blocks.text: [II, 473] Now, that the animal which the Arabs have described to us under the names ضب [ḍabb] dhab and حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun is the very same as the צב tsab of Moses is shown by so many considerations that to doubt it [II, 474] would be wrong. First, it is supported by the similarity of the Hebrew name to the Arabic. For although the Hebrew צב tsab and the Arabic ضب [ḍabb] dhab differ in sound, in both the initial letter is Tsade, which among the Arabs sounds differently because of the dot added to it. Nothing is more frequent than this change. Thus sheep, צאן tson to the Hebrews, is ضان [ḍān] dhan to the Arabs. Hyena is צבוע tsebua to the former, ضبع [ḍabuʿ] dhebu to the latter. Frog is צפרדע tsephardea to the former, ضفدع [ḍifdaʿ] dhephda to the latter. Rib is צלע tsela to the former, ضلع [ḍilʿ] dhila to the latter. Diadem, or braid of hair, is צפירה tsephira to the former, ضفيرة [ḍafīra] [col. 1054] dhephira to the latter. Dung is צפיע tsephia to the former, ضفع [ḍfʿ] dhepha to the latter. Distress is צוק tsuk to the former, ضيق [ḍīq] dhik to the latter. To laugh is צחק tsachak to the former, ضحق [ḍḥq] dhachika to the latter. 2. Secondly, that צב tsab is what we have said is made plain by the series of related animals in the same context. For in the following verse mention is made of the lizard, the stellio, the chameleon, the salamander, etc., as will be shown in its place. And there was equal reason why this species of lizard should be rejected as unclean. Nor ought it to have been omitted, since it is native to Arabia, which borders on Judaea, and is eaten among the Arabs. 3. To this is added the authority of the ancients, none of whom, I assert, took it otherwise. Certainly the four Arabic versions I was able to consult, two printed and two in manuscript, [II, 475] though they differ greatly among themselves elsewhere, here consistently have الضب [al-ḍabb] aldhab; and Onkelos has צבא tsaba, which is the Hebrew word itself, with only its ending adapted to Chaldee usage. In Jonathan, for צב tsab you read חרדונא chardona; in the Syriac ܚܕܪܘܢܐ chadrona; and in the Samaritan [?] adrona: all three come to the same thing. What is meant, namely, is the حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun of the Arabs, which Avicenna asserted above ^{c)} to be the same as the ضب [ḍabb] dhab. Some hold it to be similar to it, others its male. Damir: الحردون دويبة شبيه بالضب وقيل هو ذكر الضب لان له ذكرين مثله [al-ḥardūn duwaybba shabīh bi-l-ḍabb wa-qīla huwa dhakar al-ḍabb li-anna lahu dhakarayn mithlahu] Alchardaun (or rather alchirdaun, for he directs it to be written so) is a small animal, similar to τῷ [tō] dhab: indeed it is said to be its male, because like it it has two penises. Alcamus: الحردون لذكر الضب ودويبة احري [al-ḥardūn li-dhakar al-ḍabb wa-duwaybba aḥrī] Alchardaun is said of the male τοῦ [tou] dhab. There is also another (similar) small animal ^{(2)}.
